stem: On the Start page, where does an analyst pick the file type or server to connect to?

options.text: The Data pane on the left of a worksheet
options.rationale: The Data pane lists the fields of a data source that already exists; it is not where connections start.

options.text: The Marks card on a worksheet
options.rationale: The Marks card controls how marks look; it has nothing to do with connecting to data.

options.text: The Connect pane on the left
options.rationale: It lists the connectors for files and servers, with More for the full list.

options.text: The Extract Data dialog on the Data Source page
options.rationale: That dialog sets options for an extract of a source you have already connected to.

explanation: The Connect pane on the Start page lists the connectors: files such as Microsoft Excel and Text file, and servers for databases and cloud services. After you pick one, Tableau opens the Data Source page.

stem: Driftlight's sessions live in a busy production database. Which kind of connector does the analyst choose to reach it?

options.text: A server connector for the database
options.rationale: Databases and cloud services are listed under servers in the Connect pane.

options.text: A file connector such as Text file
options.rationale: File connectors read a local or shared file, not a database server.

options.text: The Extract Data dialog
options.rationale: That dialog configures an extract; it is not a connector.

options.text: The Data menu's Refresh command
options.rationale: Refresh updates an existing extract; it does not create a connection.

explanation: The Connect pane splits connectors into files (Microsoft Excel, Text file and others) and servers (databases and cloud services). A production database is reached through a server connector.

stem: An analyst connects to a table, drags it to the canvas and opens a sheet without touching the setting in the upper-right corner of the Data Source page. What kind of data source is it?

options.text: An extract with all rows
options.rationale: An extract is only created when Extract is selected and the settings are saved.

options.text: An extract with a sample of rows
options.rationale: Sampling is a Number of Rows option of the Extract Data dialog, which was never opened.

options.text: A saved .tdsx data source
options.rationale: A .tdsx is only created by saving the data source, which did not happen here.

options.text: A live connection
options.rationale: Unless Extract is selected, the source stays live and each view queries it directly.

explanation: In the upper-right corner of the Data Source page you can select Extract. If you don't, the data source stays a live connection and every view queries the source.

stem: A manager changes a filter on a dashboard that uses a live connection. What does Tableau do?

options.text: It reads the rows from a local .hyper file
options.rationale: A .hyper file exists only when an extract has been created.

options.text: It sends a new query to the original data source
options.rationale: With a live connection, every interaction is answered by the source.

options.text: It keeps showing the old rows until the next refresh
options.rationale: Refreshing applies to extracts; a live connection has no snapshot to refresh.

options.text: It rebuilds the data source as an extract first
options.rationale: Tableau never converts a live connection to an extract on its own.

explanation: A live connection queries the original database or file whenever the view needs data, so the speed and the freshness are those of the source.

stem: An analyst needs a connector that is not shown in the Connect pane. What should they click to see the full list?

options.text: More
options.rationale: The More link expands the Connect pane to every available connector.

options.text: Add, next to the Connections heading
options.rationale: Add attaches a second connection inside a data source that already exists.

options.text: Extract, in the upper-right corner
options.rationale: That switches an existing connection to an extract.

options.text: Add to Saved Data Sources
options.rationale: That saves an existing data source as a file.

explanation: The Connect pane shows the most common connectors. Clicking More opens the complete list of files and servers.

stem: After connecting to a file, what happens on the Data Source page before the analyst starts building a view?

options.text: Tableau automatically builds a dashboard from the first table
options.rationale: Tableau does not build views for you; the analyst builds them on a sheet.

options.text: They must create an extract before any sheet can open
options.rationale: An extract is optional; without it the connection stays live.

options.text: They drag tables to the canvas and check the preview grid
options.rationale: Then they click a sheet tab to start building.

options.text: They must save the source as a .tds file
options.rationale: Saving a data source is optional and separate from connecting.

explanation: Connecting opens the Data Source page, where you drag tables to the canvas and inspect the preview grid. Clicking a sheet tab then lets you build.

stem: Which description of a live connection is accurate?

options.text: Tableau copies all rows into a .hyper file when you connect
options.rationale: That describes an extract, not a live connection.

options.text: Tableau stores the data inside the .tds file
options.rationale: A .tds never contains data, only connection details and metadata.

options.text: Tableau works only while the source is offline
options.rationale: A live connection needs the source to be reachable.

options.text: Tableau queries the original database or file each time it needs data
options.rationale: The data stays where it is.

explanation: A live connection sends queries to the source. Nothing is copied, which is why it always shows current data but depends on the source being available.

stem: Which two connectors are file connectors in the Connect pane? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: A production database server
options.rationale: Databases are listed under servers.

options.text: Microsoft Excel
options.rationale: Excel is one of the file connectors.

options.text: A cloud service
options.rationale: Cloud services are listed under servers.

options.text: Text file
options.rationale: Text file, such as a CSV, is a file connector.

options.text: The Extract Data dialog
options.rationale: That is a dialog for extract settings, not a connector.

explanation: Files such as Microsoft Excel and Text file are one group of connectors. Servers (databases and cloud services) are the other.

stem: Which two actions are possible on the Data Source page of a new live connection? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Drag tables to the canvas
options.rationale: Tables are added to the canvas from the left pane.

options.text: Run Extract > Refresh on the extract
options.rationale: There is no extract yet, so there is nothing to refresh.

options.text: Check the data in the preview grid
options.rationale: The grid shows the rows of the tables you added.

options.text: Build a bar chart directly on the canvas
options.rationale: The canvas holds tables and their relationships; charts are built on a worksheet.

options.text: Remove the extract with Extract > Remove
options.rationale: A live connection has no extract to remove.

explanation: The Data Source page is where you shape the connection: add tables to the canvas and check the preview grid. Extract commands apply only after an extract exists.

stem: Which two statements describe a live connection? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Views show what the source holds right now
options.rationale: Each query runs against the original data.

options.text: The data is saved in a .hyper file
options.rationale: That describes an extract.

options.text: Query speed depends on the source system
options.rationale: Tableau waits for the database or file to answer.

options.text: New rows appear only after Extract > Refresh
options.rationale: Refresh applies to extracts.

options.text: The data works offline once the workbook is saved
options.rationale: A live connection needs the source to be reachable.

explanation: Because a live connection queries the original data, it is always current and as fast as the source. Snapshots, refreshes and offline use belong to extracts.

stem: An analyst creates a live connection to a text file and starts building. Which three steps are part of that process? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: Pick Text file in the Connect pane
options.rationale: The connector is the first choice.

options.text: Select Extract and click Save Settings
options.rationale: That creates an extract, not a live connection.

options.text: Point Tableau at the file
options.rationale: The file is chosen after the connector.

options.text: Right-click the source and choose Add to Saved Data Sources
options.rationale: That saves the source as a .tds or .tdsx; it is not needed to connect.

options.text: Click a sheet tab after dragging a table to the canvas
options.rationale: That starts the analysis.

options.text: Run Extract > Refresh
options.rationale: There is no extract to refresh.

explanation: Choose the connector, point it at the file, add a table and open a sheet. Extracts and saved data sources are optional extra steps.

stem: An analyst must keep working on a Driftlight workbook during a flight with no internet. Which data source type allows that?

options.text: A live connection to the production database
options.rationale: A live connection needs the source to be reachable.

options.text: An extract
options.rationale: Extracts allow for offline access to data.

options.text: A live connection to a reporting table
options.rationale: It is still a live connection and needs the server.

options.text: A cross-database join of two live connections
options.rationale: Both connections still query their sources live.

explanation: An extract is a local copy in a .hyper file, so views can be built without reaching the original source. A live connection cannot work if the source is unreachable.

stem: The operations room needs a tile that shows today's sign-ups the moment they are stored in a reporting table. What should the data source be?

options.text: An extract refreshed every night
options.rationale: A nightly snapshot is up to a day old.

options.text: An extract with an incremental refresh
options.rationale: It still shows new rows only after a refresh runs.

options.text: A .tds file with the data stored inside
options.rationale: A .tds contains no data at all.

options.text: A live connection
options.rationale: Each query returns the rows the table holds now.

explanation: When people need up-to-the-minute data and the source can answer fast enough, a live connection is the right choice. An extract is only as current as its last refresh.

stem: The production database is slow during the day and every dashboard click adds to the load. Data that is one day old is fine. What is the best option?

options.text: Use an extract and refresh it every night
options.rationale: Queries hit the extract, sparing the database.

options.text: Keep the live connection and add more filters
options.rationale: The database is still queried on every click.

options.text: Save the live connection as a .tds file
options.rationale: A .tds stores no data, so queries still go to the database.

options.text: Connect to the same table twice
options.rationale: Both connections would query the busy database.

explanation: Extracts prevent resource drains on database systems and usually give faster views. A nightly refresh keeps the snapshot fresh enough for this need.

stem: How does the data in an extract change after it is created?

options.text: Continuously, as the original source changes
options.rationale: That is how a live connection behaves.

options.text: Whenever the workbook is opened
options.rationale: Opening the workbook does not update the snapshot.

options.text: Only when the extract is refreshed
options.rationale: It is a snapshot until then.

options.text: Whenever someone filters a view
options.rationale: Filters change what is shown, not what the extract contains.

explanation: An extract is a copy saved separately from the original data, so it differs from the source until you refresh it.

stem: What does an extract use to store its data?

options.text: A .tds file
options.rationale: A .tds holds connection details and metadata but no data.

options.text: A .hyper file
options.rationale: The extract is a subset of the data saved separately from the original.

options.text: A .twb file
options.rationale: A .twb workbook holds worksheets and dashboards but no data.

options.text: A .twbx file
options.rationale: A .twbx packages a workbook with local files; it is not the extract format.

explanation: An extract is saved as a .hyper file. Workbook and data source files (.twb, .twbx, .tds, .tdsx) are different things, though packaged ones can contain an extract.

stem: The database behind a data source does not support a function the analyst wants to use in a calculation. Which approach can help?

options.text: Keep the live connection and refresh it
options.rationale: Live connections have nothing to refresh, and they depend on the source's own functions.

options.text: Save the data source as a .tds
options.rationale: A .tds saves metadata, not new functions.

options.text: Use an extract
options.rationale: Extracts can give access to functions the source does not support.

options.text: Add a second connection to the same database
options.rationale: The second connection is still limited by that database.

explanation: With a live connection you use the source's own functions. An extract can give access to functions the source doesn't support.

stem: Which feature is an advantage of a live connection over an extract?

options.text: It allows offline access
options.rationale: Offline access is an advantage of extracts.

options.text: It lets you keep only the top N rows
options.rationale: Limiting rows is an extract setting.

options.text: It reduces the load on the database
options.rationale: Live connections query the database on every interaction.

options.text: It uses the source's own functions and collation
options.rationale: The query is answered by the source itself.

explanation: A live connection hands the work to the source, so its own functions and collation apply. Offline access and lower load come with extracts.

stem: A Driftlight extract was fully refreshed at midnight. A new session row is stored in the database at 9 a.m. When does it show up in views on the extract?

options.text: After the next refresh of the extract
options.rationale: The extract is a snapshot until refreshed.

options.text: Immediately, because Tableau checks the database
options.rationale: That would be a live connection.

options.text: When a different analyst opens the workbook
options.rationale: Opening a workbook does not refresh the extract.

options.text: When the sheet tab is clicked again
options.rationale: Switching sheets redraws views from the same snapshot.

explanation: Views on an extract query the .hyper file, so changes in the original source appear only after the extract is refreshed.

stem: Which two situations favour an extract over a live connection? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The analyst must work offline
options.rationale: Extracts allow offline access.

options.text: Dashboards must show data from the last minute
options.rationale: Only a live connection gives up-to-the-minute data.

options.text: The database is busy and should not be queried on every click
options.rationale: Queries go to the extract instead.

options.text: The analyst needs the source's own collation
options.rationale: That is a reason to stay live.

options.text: The data may never be copied from the source
options.rationale: An extract is a copy of the data.

explanation: Extracts help with offline work, speed and load on the source. A live connection is better for current data and the source's own features.

stem: Which two reasons support choosing a live connection? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The data must be as current as the source
options.rationale: Each query returns the present state.

options.text: The workbook must work without network access
options.rationale: That needs an extract.

options.text: The source is fast enough to answer interactively
options.rationale: Speed is that of the source, so a fast source suits live use.

options.text: The source is slow and busy
options.rationale: That points to an extract.

options.text: A packaged copy of the data must travel with the workbook
options.rationale: Packaging data is done with extracts or packaged files.

explanation: Choose live when people need up-to-the-minute data and the database answers fast enough. Slow or busy sources and offline needs point to an extract.

stem: Which three statements about extracts compared with live connections are correct? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: An extract is stored in a .hyper file
options.rationale: It is saved separately from the original data.

options.text: Views on an extract can perform better than views on the original data
options.rationale: This is the performance benefit of extracts.

options.text: An extract can be refreshed on demand
options.rationale: Refresh updates it from the source.

options.text: A live connection keeps working with no access to its source
options.rationale: A live connection needs the source.

options.text: An extract updates itself each time a view is drawn
options.rationale: It changes only when refreshed.

options.text: A live connection stores a snapshot in a .hyper file
options.rationale: Snapshots belong to extracts.

explanation: An extract is a .hyper snapshot that is usually faster and can be refreshed when you choose. A live connection has no local copy.

stem: Where does an analyst begin creating an extract in Tableau Desktop?

options.text: Right-click the data source and choose Add to Saved Data Sources
options.rationale: That saves a .tds or .tdsx; it does not create an extract.

options.text: Click Add next to the Connections heading
options.rationale: That adds another connection to the data source.

options.text: Select Extract in the upper-right corner of the Data Source page, then click Edit
options.rationale: This opens the Extract Data dialog.

options.text: Choose Data > Extract > Refresh
options.rationale: Refresh updates an existing extract; it cannot create one.

explanation: On the Data Source page, select Extract in the upper-right corner and click Edit to open the Extract Data dialog and choose its settings.

stem: An analyst wants the extract to contain only Driftlight sessions from 2025. Which setting in the Extract Data dialog does this?

options.text: Filters
options.rationale: Filters keep only the rows you need.

options.text: Roll up dates to Year
options.rationale: That aggregates dates to a level such as month; it does not select a year.

options.text: Number of Rows set to Sample
options.rationale: A sample keeps rows chosen at random, not those of a year.

options.text: Hide All Unused Fields
options.rationale: That removes unused fields, not rows.

explanation: An extract filter works on the data before any view sees it, so rows that fail the filter are not in the extract at all.

stem: After choosing settings in the Extract Data dialog and clicking Save Settings, what starts the creation of the extract?

options.text: Choosing Data > Extract > Refresh
options.rationale: Refresh is for updating an extract that already exists.

options.text: Closing and reopening Tableau Desktop
options.rationale: Nothing is built on restart.

options.text: Selecting Live in the upper-right corner
options.rationale: That would switch the data source back to a live connection.

options.text: Clicking a sheet tab
options.rationale: Tableau builds the extract when the analyst opens a sheet.

explanation: Save Settings only stores the extract options. Clicking a sheet tab begins building the extract.

stem: An analyst hid several unneeded fields in the Data pane and wants them left out of the extract. Which option should be selected in the Extract Data dialog?

options.text: Aggregate data for visible dimensions
options.rationale: That stores pre-aggregated rows instead of every record; it is not about fields.

options.text: Hide All Unused Fields
options.rationale: Hidden fields are then left out of the extract.

options.text: Incremental refresh
options.rationale: That is a refresh method and says nothing about fields.

options.text: Physical Tables
options.rationale: That chooses how the extract stores tables, not which fields.

explanation: Hide All Unused Fields leaves hidden fields out of the extract, which makes the file smaller.

stem: Which two settings can an analyst choose in the Extract Data dialog? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Filters
options.rationale: They limit the rows kept in the extract.

options.text: Add to Saved Data Sources
options.rationale: This is a command on the data source's right-click menu.

options.text: Number of Rows: All rows, Top, or Sample
options.rationale: It limits how many rows are extracted.

options.text: Extract > History
options.rationale: That is a command on the Data menu.

options.text: Add a connection
options.rationale: Connections are added from the Connections pane.

explanation: The Extract Data dialog holds the options for the extract itself, such as filters and the number of rows. Saving sources and viewing history are separate commands.

stem: Driftlight's dashboards only ever show session trends by month, so the analyst wants the extract to store dates at month level instead of every timestamp. Which Extract Data setting does that?

options.text: Filters, with a date condition on the Start field of the sessions
options.rationale: A filter drops whole rows; it doesn't change the level of detail of the rows that remain.

options.text: Number of Rows, set to Sample so that only part of the rows is kept
options.rationale: Sample keeps only a portion of the rows; it doesn't roll dates up to a coarser level.

options.text: Aggregate data for visible dimensions, then Roll up dates to Month
options.rationale: Aggregation stores pre-aggregated rows, and Roll up dates sets the date level the extract keeps.

options.text: Incremental refresh, naming the Start field as the column for new rows
options.rationale: Incremental refresh decides how new rows are added later; it doesn't change how dates are stored.

explanation: In the Aggregation section of the Extract Data dialog, aggregating for visible dimensions stores summarised rows instead of every record, and Roll up dates lets you keep dates at a level such as month. The result is a smaller extract.

stem: The analyst wants a small test extract of a large Driftlight table, built from a portion of the rows. Where in the Extract Data dialog is that chosen?

options.text: Number of Rows, with the Sample option
options.rationale: Number of Rows offers All rows, Top N rows or a Sample.

options.text: Data Storage, with the Physical Tables option
options.rationale: Data Storage decides how tables are stored, not how many rows are kept.

options.text: Aggregation, with Roll up dates selected
options.rationale: Rolling up dates reduces date detail; it isn't a way to pick a portion of the rows.

options.text: Hide All Unused Fields, which is a check box
options.rationale: That option leaves out hidden fields (columns), not a portion of the rows.

explanation: The Number of Rows setting limits how many rows go into the extract: all of them, the top N, or a sample. Filters, aggregation and hiding fields reduce the extract in other ways.

stem: A data source joins two tables. In the Extract Data dialog, which Data Storage choice stores one table in the extract for each table in the data source's logical layer?

options.text: Physical Tables
options.rationale: Physical Tables stores one table per physical table, which is the other choice.

options.text: Aggregate data for visible dimensions
options.rationale: That is an Aggregation option, not a Data Storage choice.

options.text: All rows
options.rationale: That is a Number of Rows option and has nothing to do with how tables are stored.

options.text: Logical Tables
options.rationale: Logical Tables stores one table per logical table.

explanation: Data Storage has two choices: Logical Tables, with one extract table per logical table, and Physical Tables, with one per physical table. The other settings in the dialog are filters, aggregation, number of rows, incremental refresh and hiding unused fields.

stem: A Driftlight extract uses incremental refresh with a column that identifies new rows. Later, a value in an old session row is corrected in the source database. What happens at the next incremental refresh?

options.text: The corrected row is updated, because Tableau compares every row with the source
options.rationale: That describes a full refresh; incremental refresh doesn't compare existing rows.

options.text: The corrected old row isn't updated; only rows new since the last refresh are added
options.rationale: Incremental refresh only includes new rows since the previous refresh.

options.text: The whole extract is replaced with the latest data from the source
options.rationale: Replacing everything is what a full refresh does, and it is the default.

options.text: The refresh fails, because incremental refresh can't be used after a data change
options.rationale: Corrections to old rows don't make it fail; they are simply not picked up.

explanation: An incremental refresh adds only the rows that are new since the previous refresh, found through the column you chose. Changes to rows already in the extract are not picked up, so use a full refresh when old rows can change.

stem: Which two statements about incremental refresh of an extract are correct? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: It only includes rows that are new since the previous refresh
options.rationale: That is what makes it incremental, as opposed to a full refresh.

options.text: It replaces all the data in the extract with the latest information
options.rationale: That describes a full refresh, which is the default.

options.text: It picks up edits made to rows that are already in the extract
options.rationale: Only new rows are added; existing rows stay as they were.

options.text: It needs a column that identifies new rows, and Number of Rows set to All rows
options.rationale: You name the column in the dialog, and the option needs All rows.

options.text: It works together with Aggregate data for visible dimensions
options.rationale: Incremental refresh can't be used together with aggregation.

explanation: Incremental refresh uses a column you name to find new rows and adds only those. It requires All rows and can't be combined with aggregation, and it doesn't update rows already in the extract.

stem: Which two actions are in the Extract submenu of the Data menu for a data source that has an extract? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: History, to see the past refreshes of the extract
options.rationale: Extract > History lists the refreshes.

options.text: Add, to connect a second connection to the data source
options.rationale: A second connection is added with Add in the Connections pane, not in the Extract submenu.

options.text: Remove, to remove the extract from the data source
options.rationale: Extract > Remove removes the extract.

options.text: Add to Saved Data Sources, to create a .tds file
options.rationale: That is on the data source's right-click menu at the top of the Data pane.

options.text: Package, to turn the workbook into a .twbx
options.rationale: Packaging a workbook is a File menu task, not an extract action.

explanation: With the data source selected, the Data menu has an Extract submenu: Refresh, History and Remove. Saving data sources and adding connections happen elsewhere.

stem: A lead analyst wants to reuse renamed fields and calculated fields in other workbooks, saving the connection details but no rows. Which file type should be saved?

options.text: .hyper
options.rationale: A .hyper file holds the extracted data itself, not a reusable set of metadata.

options.text: .twbx
options.rationale: A packaged workbook zips a workbook with its local data; it isn't a data source file.

options.text: .tds
options.rationale: A Tableau data source file saves the connection and the metadata, without the data.

options.text: .tdsx
options.rationale: A packaged data source also contains a copy of the local data or extracts, which was not wanted.

explanation: A .tds file contains the connection information and metadata such as calculated fields, groups, sets, bins, default properties and renamed fields. It does not contain the data itself.

stem: Where does an analyst start saving a data source as a .tds so that colleagues can reuse it?

options.text: Right-click a worksheet tab, then choose Save as Data Source
options.rationale: Worksheet tabs offer worksheet actions; the data source is saved from the Data pane.

options.text: Right-click the data source's name at the top of the Data pane, then choose Add to Saved Data Sources
options.rationale: That is the path to the Save dialog where you choose .tds or .tdsx.

options.text: Open the Data menu, then choose Extract > Save Settings
options.rationale: The Extract submenu manages refreshes and the extract itself; it doesn't save the data source.

options.text: Open the File menu, then choose Save to save the workbook
options.rationale: Saving the workbook creates a .twb, which isn't a reusable data source file.

explanation: At the top of the Data pane, right-click the data source name and select Add to Saved Data Sources. Then enter a file name, choose .tds or .tdsx and click Save.

stem: A Driftlight analyst must send a colleague, who can't reach the original files, a data source with its metadata and the local data. Which file type fits?

options.text: .tds
options.rationale: A .tds holds the connection and metadata but no data, so the colleague still wouldn't have the rows.

options.text: .twb
options.rationale: A workbook file holds worksheets, dashboards and stories, and no data.

options.text: .hyper
options.rationale: A .hyper file holds extracted data, but not the metadata the colleague also needs.

options.text: .tdsx
options.rationale: A packaged data source contains the .tds contents plus a copy of the local file-based data or extracts.

explanation: A .tdsx is the packaged version of a data source: it includes everything in the .tds and a copy of local file data or extracts. Use it when the data has to travel with the metadata.

stem: By default, where does Tableau Desktop save a data source added with Add to Saved Data Sources?

options.text: In the Datasources folder of My Tableau Repository
options.rationale: The repository is created in the Documents folder, and the Datasources folder is the default save location.

options.text: In the Workbooks folder of My Tableau Repository, beside saved workbooks
options.rationale: The Workbooks folder is for workbooks, not saved data sources.

options.text: Next to the original file that holds the data, in the same folder
options.rationale: Tableau doesn't use the location of the source file as the default.

options.text: On Tableau Public, as a shared extract for other people to download
options.rationale: Saving a data source through this command creates a local file, not a public upload.

explanation: The save dialog opens in the Datasources folder of My Tableau Repository, which Tableau creates in your Documents folder. You can choose another folder if you prefer.

stem: Which item is stored in a .tds file?

options.text: Every session row from the source CSV files
options.rationale: A .tds never contains the data itself.

options.text: The worksheets and dashboards built on the data
options.rationale: Worksheets and dashboards belong in a workbook file, not a data source file.

options.text: The rows of an extract built from the data source
options.rationale: Extract data lives in a .hyper file or inside a packaged .tdsx, not in a .tds.

options.text: A calculated field in the data source
options.rationale: Calculated fields are metadata and are kept in the data source file.

explanation: A .tds saves the connection information and metadata: groups, sets, calculated fields, bins, default properties such as number formats and sort order, and renamed fields. Worksheets and the data itself are not part of it.

stem: What does a packaged workbook (.twbx) contain?

options.text: Only the connection details and the metadata of one data source
options.rationale: That describes a .tds, which doesn't hold a workbook.

options.text: A workbook, plus any local file data and background images, in one zip file
options.rationale: That is the definition of a packaged workbook.

options.text: Only the extracted data, with no worksheets or dashboards
options.rationale: That describes a .hyper extract.

options.text: Worksheets, dashboards and stories, but never any data
options.rationale: That describes an unpackaged workbook (.twb), which has no data.

explanation: A .twb holds the worksheets, dashboards and stories only. A .twbx zips that workbook with local file data and background images, so it can be opened on a machine without the original files.

stem: Which of these does a .tdsx contain that a plain .tds does not?

options.text: The default number formats that were set on fields
options.rationale: Default properties are metadata, so a plain .tds already has them.

options.text: The calculated fields added to the data source
options.rationale: Calculations are metadata and are stored in the plain .tds too.

options.text: A copy of any local file-based data or extracts
options.rationale: The packaged version adds the local data, which the plain data source file never holds.

options.text: The connection information that points to the data
options.rationale: Connection information is part of every data source file, packaged or not.

explanation: A .tdsx has everything a .tds has, plus a copy of local file data or extracts. The metadata and connection information are in both.

stem: Which three items are saved in a Tableau data source file (.tds)? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: Calculated fields
options.rationale: Calculations are metadata and are stored.

options.text: The rows of the original table
options.rationale: A .tds holds no data.

options.text: Default number formats for fields
options.rationale: Default field properties are saved as metadata.

options.text: Worksheets and dashboards
options.rationale: Those are stored in a workbook, not a data source file.

options.text: Groups, sets and bins
options.rationale: Groups, sets and bins are part of the saved metadata.

options.text: Background images for dashboards
options.rationale: Background images are packaged in a .twbx workbook.

explanation: A .tds stores the connection information plus metadata such as calculated fields, groups, sets, bins and default field properties. Data, worksheets and images are not in it.

stem: In the Save dialog opened by Add to Saved Data Sources, which two file types can be chosen? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Tableau Data Source (.tds)
options.rationale: The unpackaged data source file.

options.text: Tableau Workbook (.twb)
options.rationale: Workbooks are saved from the File menu, not as saved data sources.

options.text: Tableau Hyper Extract (.hyper)
options.rationale: A .hyper file is created by extracting data, not by saving a data source.

options.text: Tableau Packaged Workbook (.twbx)
options.rationale: Packaged workbooks are created by saving a workbook.

options.text: Tableau Packaged Data Source (.tdsx)
options.rationale: The packaged data source includes local data or extracts.

explanation: Add to Saved Data Sources asks for a file name and a choice between .tds and .tdsx, then saves to the Datasources folder by default.

stem: Which two statements about Tableau file types are correct? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: A .tds contains the actual data of the data source
options.rationale: A .tds only contains the information needed to connect to the data.

options.text: A .twbx contains a workbook and its supporting local file data
options.rationale: It is a zip file with the workbook and local data and images.

options.text: A .twb contains local file data and background images
options.rationale: That is what the packaged .twbx adds; a .twb has no data.

options.text: A .tdsx contains a copy of any local data or extracts
options.rationale: That is what separates it from a .tds.

options.text: A .hyper file stores the connection and the metadata of a data source
options.rationale: A .hyper file stores extracted data.

explanation: The packaged formats, .twbx and .tdsx, add local data to their unpackaged counterparts. The .twb and .tds hold definitions only, and a .hyper holds extracted data.

stem: A Driftlight analyst is on the Data Source page with the sessions CSV on the canvas and now wants to connect to the Excel targets file in the same data source. What should the analyst click?

options.text: New Data Source on the Data menu, then drag the Excel tables across
options.rationale: That creates a separate data source, which can't be joined to the first one.

options.text: Add, to the right of the Connections heading in the left pane
options.rationale: Add creates a second connection inside the current data source.

options.text: Extract in the upper-right corner of the Data Source page
options.rationale: That switches the data source to an extract; it adds no connection.

options.text: More in the Connect pane of the Start page
options.rationale: That lists more connector types on the Start page; it doesn't add a connection to the open data source.

explanation: The Add link next to Connections creates a second connection in the same data source, rather than an entirely different one. Then you connect to the Excel file as usual.

stem: After adding a second connection to the Excel targets file, what does the analyst do to bring its data in?

options.text: Build a view with the targets on a separate worksheet, then switch off the first connection
options.rationale: Each connection stays in the data source and nothing needs switching off.

options.text: Save the first connection as a .tds, then reopen it with the Excel file inside
options.rationale: A .tds doesn't hold data, so it can't merge the Excel file in.

options.text: Select Extract on both connections so that Tableau merges the files
options.rationale: Making an extract doesn't combine tables; you still need a join or relationship.

options.text: Drag a table from the new connection to the canvas and relate or join it
options.rationale: The new table joins the existing table in the same data source.

explanation: With the second connection in place, you drag a table from it onto the canvas and relate or join it to a table from the first connection. Both connections then belong to one data source.

stem: In a data source with two connections, how does Tableau show which connection a table or column belongs to?

options.text: It colours the tables on the canvas and the columns in the grid
options.rationale: Tableau colours them to show which connection the data comes from.

options.text: It adds the name of the connection to the start of every field name
options.rationale: Field names are not changed by connections.

options.text: It puts each connection's fields on a separate worksheet automatically
options.rationale: Fields from all connections are available in the same data source.

options.text: It hides the fields of the connection that was added first in the pane
options.rationale: Nothing is hidden; both connections' fields can be used.

explanation: Tableau colours the canvas tables and the data grid columns so that you can see their connection. This helps when several files or databases are combined.

stem: An analyst opens the Excel targets file through a new data source in the Data menu and then tries to join it to the sessions tables. Why can't that work?

options.text: Excel files can't be joined to anything other than other Excel files
options.rationale: Tables from different files and databases can be joined within one data source.

options.text: Joins are only possible when both sources are extracts
options.rationale: Cross-database joins work with live connections too.

options.text: Separate data sources can't be joined; both tables must be in one data source as two connections
options.rationale: A cross-database join needs the tables in one data source.

options.text: Targets files must first be saved as a .tdsx before they can be joined
options.rationale: File types for saving data sources have no effect on joining.

explanation: Two separate data sources can't be joined; they can only be combined in a view by blending. To join across files or databases, add the second source with Add in the Connections pane so both are connections in one data source.

stem: What is a join between tables from two different connections in one data source called?

options.text: A data blend, which combines separate data sources in a view
options.rationale: Blending combines separate data sources in a view; it isn't a join in a data source.

options.text: A relationship, a flexible way to combine tables on the canvas
options.rationale: Relationships are a way to combine tables on the canvas, but they aren't the name for a join across connections.

options.text: A union, which appends the rows of tables with matching columns
options.rationale: A union appends rows of tables with matching columns; it doesn't match rows across keys.

options.text: A cross-database join
options.rationale: That is the name for joining tables from different connections.

explanation: Joining tables that come from different connections is a cross-database join. It lets one data source combine, say, a CSV and an Excel workbook.

stem: Which data source typically does not support cross-database joins?

options.text: A Microsoft Excel workbook with a targets sheet
options.rationale: Excel files can be joined to other connections, such as a CSV file.

options.text: A text file such as one of the sessions CSV files
options.rationale: Text files can be one side of a cross-database join.

options.text: A published Tableau data source
options.rationale: Published data sources are among the sources that don't support cross-database joins.

options.text: A relational database server that holds a sessions table
options.rationale: Tables from two databases can be joined with a cross-database join.

explanation: Not every source supports cross-database joins. Cube data, most extract-only connectors and published Tableau data sources are among those that don't.

stem: Which statement about the speed of joins is correct?

options.text: Cross-database joins are always faster, because Tableau processes them locally
options.rationale: They're not always faster; joins in one database are usually quicker.

options.text: Joins within a single database are usually faster than cross-database joins
options.rationale: Tableau's help notes this.

options.text: Joins are always equally fast, whatever the connections
options.rationale: Where the tables come from does affect speed.

options.text: Joins are only possible within a single database
options.rationale: Cross-database joins are possible, but they come with limits.

explanation: A cross-database join has to combine data from different connections, so joins within a single database are usually faster. That is a reason to keep related tables in one database when you can.

stem: Which two statements about adding a second connection to a data source are correct? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: It creates a second connection rather than an entirely different data source
options.rationale: That is how Tableau describes the Add link.

options.text: It adds a new data source to the Data pane next to the first
options.rationale: A new data source comes from the Data menu, not from Add in the Connections pane.

options.text: Tables and columns are coloured to show which connection they come from
options.rationale: The canvas and the data grid use colour for the connection.

options.text: Both connections must use the same connector type
options.rationale: A CSV file and an Excel workbook can sit in one data source.

options.text: Both connections must be extracts
options.rationale: Live connections can be combined too.

explanation: Add in the Connections pane keeps everything in one data source, with Tableau colouring tables and columns by connection. The connectors can be different, such as a text file and an Excel workbook.

stem: Which two sources are among those that usually do not support cross-database joins? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Cube data
options.rationale: Cube data is one of the sources listed as not supporting them.

options.text: A text file
options.rationale: Text files can be joined to other connections.

options.text: A Microsoft Excel workbook
options.rationale: Excel workbooks work in cross-database joins.

options.text: A published Tableau data source
options.rationale: Published data sources are also on the list.

options.text: A relational database server
options.rationale: Relational databases support cross-database joins.

explanation: Cube data, most extract-only connectors and published Tableau data sources don't support cross-database joins. Common file and database connectors do.

stem: Which three steps are part of creating a data source that uses multiple connections? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: Connect to the first source and drag a table to the canvas
options.rationale: This is the starting point.

options.text: Click Add next to the Connections heading and connect to the second source
options.rationale: This adds the second connection to the same data source.

options.text: Choose New Data Source on the Data menu for the second source
options.rationale: That makes a separate data source, which can't be joined.

options.text: Drag a table from the new connection onto the canvas and relate or join it to the first
options.rationale: This is how the two connections are combined.

options.text: Select Extract on the first connection and reconnect the second
options.rationale: Extracting is not part of combining connections.

options.text: Save the first connection as a .tdsx and import it into the second
options.rationale: Saving a data source doesn't combine connections.

explanation: Connect to the first source, add the second with Add in the Connections pane, then drag a table from the new connection onto the canvas and relate or join it. New Data Source would create a second data source.
